units.title: Probability Spaces
units.blurb: Build probability from three rules, and count carefully when outcomes are equally likely.

units.title: Conditioning
units.blurb: Tell joint from conditional probability, split problems into cases, update with Bayes' theorem, and test independence.

units.title: Discrete Random Variables
units.blurb: Work with pmfs and CDFs, expectations of functions, variance rules and indicators, and the classic discrete distributions.

units.title: Continuous Random Variables
units.blurb: Find probabilities, CDFs, means and variances from densities, meet the exponential distribution and the Poisson process, and transform variables.

units.title: Joint Distributions
units.blurb: Handle two random variables at once: joint tables and densities, conditional distributions, covariance, sums and conditional expectation.

units.title: Inequalities and Limit Theorems
units.blurb: Bound probabilities with Markov and Chebyshev, then see why averages settle down and sums look normal.

units.title: Markov Chains
units.blurb: Follow a process that moves between states at random: n-step probabilities, absorption and the long run.

topics.title: The Axioms of Probability
topics.short: Every probability rule follows from three: P(A) ≥ 0, P(S) = 1, and the probabilities of disjoint events add.
topics.trouble: Students accept an assignment of probabilities that adds to more than 1, or add P(A) + P(B) for events that overlap.

topics.title: Inclusion–Exclusion for Events
topics.short: P(A ∪ B ∪ C) adds the three probabilities, subtracts the three pairwise overlaps and adds back the triple overlap.
topics.trouble: Students forget to add back P(A ∩ B ∩ C) after subtracting the pairs.

topics.title: Products of Chances: The Birthday Problem
topics.short: Find "at least one match" through its complement, a product of shrinking fractions: in a group of 23, a shared birthday is slightly more likely than not.
topics.trouble: Students multiply 1/365 by the number of people, or compare everyone with one chosen person, when every pair of people could match.

topics.title: Conditional or Joint?
topics.short: P(A ∩ B) is the chance that both happen; P(A ∣ B) is the chance of A among the outcomes where B happens. Read the question to see which one it asks for.
topics.trouble: Students answer with the joint probability P(A ∩ B) when the question asks "of those with B, what fraction have A?", or divide by the wrong event.

topics.title: The Law of Total Probability
topics.short: Split into cases A₁, …, Aₙ that cover every outcome without overlapping: P(B) = Σ P(B ∣ Aᵢ) P(Aᵢ).
topics.trouble: Students add the conditional probabilities P(B ∣ Aᵢ) without weighting each one by P(Aᵢ).

topics.title: Bayes' Theorem with Several Causes
topics.short: P(Aⱼ ∣ B) = P(B ∣ Aⱼ) P(Aⱼ) / Σ P(B ∣ Aᵢ) P(Aᵢ), and each new piece of evidence updates the answer again.
topics.trouble: Students use P(B ∣ A) as if it were P(A ∣ B), or forget to divide by P(B).

topics.title: Independence of Several Events
topics.short: A, B and C are independent when every pair and the triple multiply; disjoint events with positive probabilities are never independent.
topics.trouble: Students treat mutually exclusive events as independent, though knowing one happened rules out the other. Others check only pairs: for two coin flips, "first is heads," "second is heads" and "the flips match" are independent in pairs but not all three together.

topics.title: PMFs and CDFs
topics.short: A pmf lists P(X = x); the CDF F(x) = P(X ≤ x) climbs in steps, and P(a < X ≤ b) = F(b) − F(a).
topics.trouble: Students use F(b) − F(a) for P(a ≤ X ≤ b) with a discrete X, which leaves out P(X = a).

topics.title: Expected Value of a Function
topics.short: E[g(X)] = Σ g(x) P(X = x), and in general E[g(X)] ≠ g(E[X]).
topics.trouble: Students find E[X²] by squaring E[X].

topics.title: Variance: The Shortcut and the Rules
topics.short: Var(X) = E[X²] − (E[X])², and Var(aX + b) = a² Var(X).
topics.trouble: Students write Var(aX + b) = a Var(X) + b, which makes Var(−X) negative.

topics.title: Linearity of Expectation and Indicators
topics.short: E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y] always, so a count has mean equal to the sum of its indicators' probabilities: a shuffled deck has on average 1 card left in its starting place.
topics.trouble: Students think adding expected values needs independence, and give up on counts built from dependent pieces.

topics.title: Sampling without Replacement: The Hypergeometric Distribution
topics.short: Drawing n from N items, K of them successes: P(X = k) = C(K, k) C(N − K, n − k) / C(N, n).
topics.trouble: Students use the binomial distribution when drawing without replacement from a small group, where the draws are not independent.

topics.title: Waiting for the rth Success
topics.short: The number of trials needed for r successes has P(X = k) = C(k − 1, r − 1) pʳ (1 − p)^(k − r) and mean r/p.
topics.trouble: Students use C(k, r) instead of C(k − 1, r − 1), forgetting that the last trial must be the rth success.

topics.title: The Poisson Distribution
topics.short: Counts of rare events in a fixed time or space: P(X = k) = e^(−λ) λᵏ / k!, with mean and variance both λ.
topics.trouble: Students keep the same λ when the time window changes: 3 per hour means λ = 6 for two hours.

topics.title: The Poisson Approximation to the Binomial
topics.short: When n is large and p is small, Binomial(n, p) is close to Poisson with λ = np.
topics.trouble: Students use the approximation when p is not small, where it can be far off.

topics.title: Choosing a Distribution
topics.short: Match the story to binomial, geometric, negative binomial, hypergeometric or Poisson.
topics.trouble: Students reach for the binomial whenever there are "successes," without checking for a fixed number of independent trials with the same p.

topics.title: Probability Density Functions
topics.short: A density f ≥ 0 has total area 1, and P(a ≤ X ≤ b) = ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx.
topics.trouble: Students read f(x) as a probability. A density can be larger than 1 (f(x) = 4 on [0, 1/4]), and P(X = a) = 0 for every single value a.

topics.title: CDFs, Medians and Percentiles
topics.short: F(x) = ∫ f(t) dt from −∞ to x, f = F′, and the median m solves F(m) = 1/2.
topics.trouble: Students build F(x) for a piecewise density from the current piece alone, leaving out the area of the pieces to its left.

topics.title: Mean and Variance of a Continuous Variable
topics.short: E[X] = ∫ x f(x) dx and E[g(X)] = ∫ g(x) f(x) dx, and the variance shortcut still holds.
topics.trouble: Students integrate f(x) alone and get 1, forgetting the factor x.

topics.title: The Exponential Distribution
topics.short: f(x) = λe^(−λx) for x ≥ 0 has mean 1/λ, and it is memoryless: P(X > s + t ∣ X > s) = P(X > t).
topics.trouble: Students use the rate λ as the mean, or expect a part that has already lasted a long time to be "due" to fail.

topics.title: The Poisson Process
topics.short: For random arrivals at rate λ, the count in a window of length t is Poisson with mean λt, and the gaps between arrivals are exponential with mean 1/λ.
topics.trouble: Students give the count in time t the mean λ instead of λt, or give the gaps the mean λ instead of 1/λ.

topics.title: Densities of Functions of a Variable
topics.short: Find the density of Y = g(X) through its CDF: work out F_Y(y) = P(g(X) ≤ y), then differentiate.
topics.trouble: Students substitute into the density, f_Y(y) = f_X(g⁻¹(y)), and lose the factor from the derivative, so the new "density" no longer has area 1.

topics.title: Joint and Marginal Distributions
topics.short: A joint table gives P(X = x, Y = y); add across a row or down a column to get the marginal distributions.
topics.trouble: Students read one cell of the joint table as a marginal probability.

topics.title: Conditional Distributions and Independent Variables
topics.short: P(X = x ∣ Y = y) divides a row of the joint table by the row's total; X and Y are independent when every cell equals the product of its marginals.
topics.trouble: Students check one cell and declare X and Y independent. Every cell must factor.

topics.title: Uniform Points and Geometric Probability
topics.short: When a point is uniform in a region, probability is area over total area: two numbers chosen uniformly from [0, 1] differ by less than 1/4 with probability 7/16.
topics.trouble: Students work with lengths on one axis instead of areas in the square of possible pairs.

topics.title: Joint Densities
topics.short: P((X, Y) ∈ R) = ∬_R f(x, y) dA; set up the limits for regions such as {x < y}.
topics.trouble: Students integrate over the whole support instead of the part where the event happens, or forget that f is 0 outside its support.

topics.title: Marginal and Conditional Densities
topics.short: f_X(x) = ∫ f(x, y) dy, and X and Y are independent when f(x, y) = f_X(x) f_Y(y) everywhere.
topics.trouble: Students call f(x, y) = 2 on the triangle 0 < x < y < 1 a product of separate functions. Its support is not a rectangle, so X and Y are dependent.

topics.title: Covariance and Correlation
topics.short: Cov(X, Y) = E[XY] − E[X]E[Y], and the correlation ρ = Cov(X, Y)/(σ_X σ_Y) lies between −1 and 1.
topics.trouble: Students think zero covariance means independence. If X is −1, 0 or 1 with equal chances and Y = X², then Cov(X, Y) = 0, yet Y depends on X.

topics.title: Variance of a Sum
topics.short: Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) + 2 Cov(X, Y), and the variance of a longer sum adds every pairwise covariance.
topics.trouble: Students drop the covariance terms when the variables are dependent, as with the indicators of a shuffled deck.

topics.title: Sums of Independent Variables
topics.short: The distribution of X + Y comes from adding over every split: P(X + Y = s) = Σ P(X = k) P(Y = s − k), with an integral for densities.
topics.trouble: Students add the two pmfs or densities instead of convolving them. The sum of two independent uniform variables has a triangular density, not a uniform one.

topics.title: Conditional Expectation
topics.short: E[X ∣ Y = y] averages X within one slice, and E[X] = E[E[X ∣ Y]] averages the slices.
topics.trouble: Students average the conditional means without weighting them by the probabilities of the slices.

topics.title: Maximum and Minimum of Independent Variables
topics.short: P(max ≤ x) = F(x)ⁿ and P(min > x) = (1 − F(x))ⁿ; the minimum of independent exponential variables is exponential with the rates added.
topics.trouble: Students write P(max ≤ x) as n · F(x), or try to find P(min ≤ x) directly instead of through its complement.

topics.title: Markov's and Chebyshev's Inequalities
topics.short: For X ≥ 0, P(X ≥ a) ≤ E[X]/a; for any X with mean μ and standard deviation σ, P(|X − μ| ≥ kσ) ≤ 1/k².
topics.trouble: Students read the bound as the exact probability, or use Markov's inequality for a variable that can be negative.

topics.title: The Law of Large Numbers
topics.short: The average of n independent trials has variance σ²/n, so it settles near μ as n grows.
topics.trouble: Students expect the next results to "make up" for a streak. The average settles because the early results are swamped by many later ones, not corrected.

topics.title: Moment Generating Functions
topics.short: M(t) = E[e^(tX)]; its derivatives at t = 0 give E[X], E[X²], …, and the MGF of a sum of independent variables is the product of their MGFs.
topics.trouble: Students read M″(0) as the variance. It is E[X²], and Var(X) = M″(0) − (M′(0))².

topics.title: The Central Limit Theorem for Sums
topics.short: A sum of n independent copies of X is close to normal, with mean nμ and standard deviation σ√n.
topics.trouble: Students use σn or σ/√n for the spread of a sum. For a sum it is σ√n; σ/√n belongs to the average.

topics.title: The Normal Approximation to the Binomial
topics.short: Approximate Binomial(n, p) with a normal curve, widening each whole number to an interval of width 1: P(X ≤ 12) ≈ P(Y < 12.5).
topics.trouble: Students skip the continuity correction, or move the boundary the wrong way: P(X < 12) = P(X ≤ 11) ≈ P(Y < 11.5).

topics.title: Markov Chains and Transition Matrices
topics.short: The next state depends only on the current one; a row of probabilities times the transition matrix P steps forward, so after n steps the distribution is π₀Pⁿ.
topics.trouble: Students multiply on the wrong side (Pπ₀ with a row-based P), or write rows that do not add to 1.

topics.title: Absorption and First-Step Analysis
topics.short: Condition on the first step to get equations for the chance of absorption and the expected time to get there, as in the gambler's ruin.
topics.trouble: Students forget to add 1 for the step just taken when writing the equations for expected times.

topics.title: Stationary Distributions
topics.short: Solve πP = π together with π₁ + ⋯ + πₙ = 1 to find the long-run share of time spent in each state.
topics.trouble: Students solve πP = π but drop the condition that π adds to 1, so they report a multiple of the answer (or none, since π = 0 also solves πP = π).
